notes.title: Chapter map: Concurrency in LLD

headings.text: 🌳 Which tool for this concurrency problem?

notes.html:
Assume every LLD problem ends with "now make it thread-safe". Item 27 is the judgment; 28–31 are the locking toolkit; 32–33 are the half that isn't about locks. Read each arrow as a sentence: the contended resource picks optimistic or pessimistic locking.

Green = 🔴 CORE, blue = 🟡 SUPPORTING, yellow = 🟢 BREADTH.

Reading order:27 contended resource28 optimistic vs pessimistic29 lock granularity30 ConcurrentHashMap atomics31 lock ordering32 idempotency keys33 hold, then confirm34 background schedulers

Owners

Idea Owner note
Naming the one contended resource (seat, slot, count) and locking only that 27
Version or compare-and-set retry against a lock; the unique constraint as the last line of defence 28
Per-show, per-floor or per-slot locks, and what that does to throughput 29
compute and putIfAbsent as the atomic step; "the map is storage, not the lock" 30
A global order by ID when one operation takes two locks 31
A retried "book" or "pay" must not act twice: a dedupe key, not a lock 32
A hold with a time limit; sweeper against expiry-on-read 33
ScheduledExecutorService: shutdown, missed ticks, a task that dies silently 34
The intent method that a lock wraps item 10, not these notes
An injected clock, which makes every time-limit path testable item 38, not these notes
A test that really races two threads item 41, not these notes
The booking lifecycle as a state machine state, not these notes

Which tool for this concurrency problem?

Notes 28–33 own the reasoning. The first question is the binding one, because a retry isn't a race and no lock fixes it.

Read down and stop at the first yes.

  • 🪪 Idempotency key (32): if the two requests are different users after the same seat, it is a race; go on down the tree.
  • Hold with a time limit (33): if the whole action completes in one call, you don't need a hold.
  • Fixed lock order (31): if one coarser lock covers both and throughput allows it, that is simpler.
  • 🔐 A lock per resource (28, 29): if there is more than one server, the in-process lock isn't enough; add the database constraint.
  • Atomic compute, or version and retry (30, 28): if retries pile up under load, switch to a lock.

At a glance

Item Use it when The sentence to say
27 always, first "the contended resource is X; everything else is read-mostly"
28 two users, one resource "lock in one JVM; the unique constraint across several"
29 one global lock is the bottleneck "one lock per show, not one for the system"
30 a check-then-act on one key "compute makes the check and the write one step"
31 an operation takes two locks "always acquire in ID order"
32 a client may retry "the key is stored before the side effect"
33 a seat is held while the user pays "held with an expiry; released by a sweeper or on read"
34 something must happen later "a scheduled executor, with shutdown and failure handled"

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: find the one thing two threads fight over and protect only that. Half of what looks like concurrency is retries and time limits, which locks don't solve.
  • The two most-confused pairs: a race vs a retry (28 vs 32) · optimistic vs pessimistic (28: detect and retry vs prevent).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the tree above and the three sentences in this folder's README.
  • Cross-section links: what gets locked is defined in §2; how it is tested, in §5; the Java primitives are in 08-java/06-Concurrency/.

notes.title: Identify the Contended Resource First
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
First move on "now make it thread-safe"? Name the one contended resource. Lock only that.
What's contended in booking / parking / elevator / inventory? The ShowSeat; the ParkingSpot; the request queue; the count.
What's not contended? Read-mostly metadata — Movie, Theatre, Screen, Show. Immutable after load.
Where is the race, precisely? Between the check and the write.
The three shapes of fix? Make check+write indivisible; prevent the second thread entering; let both proceed and one fail at a constraint.

The 30-Second Answer

Every LLD problem has exactly one place where two threads collide, and almost everything else in the object graph is read-mostly or thread-confined. The mid-level answer is synchronized on the service method — correct, and it serialises the world. The senior answer names the resource, locks precisely that, and states the throughput consequence before being asked.

Locating It

The mechanical procedure: for each piece of mutable state, ask whether two concurrent user actions can target the same instance. Almost always the answer is yes for exactly one class.

Problem Contended Not contended
BookMyShow ShowSeat status Movie, Theatre, Screen, Show metadata
Parking lot ParkingSpot occupancy Vehicle, FeeSchedule, Level layout
Elevator the request queue per car Building, Floor, Display config
Flash sale the stock count product catalogue
Splitwise the balance edge between two users User, Group membership
LRU cache the map + recency list together capacity, the eviction policy object

Note the last one: sometimes the contended resource is two structures that must move together, which is why an LRU needs one lock covering both rather than a concurrent map plus a concurrent list.

Where the Race Actually Is

// Thread A and Thread B, interleaved:
if (seat.status() == AVAILABLE) {     // A reads AVAILABLE
                                      // B reads AVAILABLE
    seat.hold(user);                  // A writes HELD
                                      // B writes HELD  ← two holders, one seat
}

The window is between the check and the write, it's microseconds wide, and the failure is silent — two confirmations, one seat, discovered at the door. Naming the window precisely is what tells you the shape of the fix, and there are only three:

  1. Make check-and-write one indivisible operation — compute, putIfAbsent, a CAS on a version, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (→ items 28, 30).
  2. Prevent the second thread from entering — a lock held across both (→ item 29).
  3. Let both proceed, one fails at a constraint — a unique index on the contended key (→ item 28).

Failure Mode

synchronized on the booking service. Correct and useless: it serialises every show in every theatre. If you start there for a working skeleton, say so and say what you'll narrow it to.

Locking read-mostly metadata. Costs throughput and tells the interviewer you didn't find the resource.

Not saying the consequence. "Per-seat locks" is a choice. "Per-seat, because a per-show lock serialises a 300-seat house at one booking at a time" is a defended choice.

Connections

  • Next: 28-optimistic-vs-pessimistic-locking.md
  • Depends on: ../02-oo-design-principles/10-encapsulation-of-invariants.md — the intent method is the unit you lock.
  • Worked: ../../07-Design-problems/book-my-show.md · ../../07-Design-problems/high-concurrency-flash-sale-system.md

notes.title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Isolation levels, row locks, and where optimistic conflicts surface — PostgreSQL Docs: Transaction Isolation

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The deciding variable? Contention rate — how often two threads actually want the same row.
Optimistic degrades when? Under high contention: every loser does the work and discards it, adding load exactly when busy.
Pessimistic costs what? Waiting threads — which makes lock granularity the whole design (→ item 29).
Seat booking — which? Pessimistic per (show, seat) for the hold.
And the sentence that lands the answer? Plus a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) — the in-process lock is decorative the moment there are two replicas.

The 30-Second Answer

Pessimistic locks before reading and holds until the write, so the second thread waits; optimistic reads a version, does the work, and writes conditionally on that version being unchanged, retrying on conflict. Contention rate picks between them. Hot seat at on-sale time: pessimistic, because optimistic retries pile load onto the moment of peak load. Rarely-touched record with a long critical section: optimistic, because the collision almost never happens and holding a lock across that work is worse.

The Trade-off in Full

Pessimistic — right when contention is real and the critical section is short. A seat on a popular show is exactly that: many threads, one row, microseconds of work inside. The cost is that a thread holding the lock is a thread everyone waits behind, so granularity becomes the design: per (show, seat) is fine, per Show serialises a full house, per service serialises the chain.

Optimistic — right when contention is rare or the critical section is long or spans an external call. Profile updates, config changes, anything where the probability of collision is low enough that the retry path almost never runs. Under high contention it inverts: N threads do the work, N−1 throw it away and retry, and the retry storm arrives at the worst moment.

// Optimistic: version guard, retry loop, bounded.
for (int attempt = 0; attempt < MAX; attempt++) {
    ShowSeat s = repo.find(key).orElseThrow();
    long seen = s.version();
    ShowSeat next = s.withHold(user, clock);          // work done outside any lock
    if (repo.saveIfVersion(next, seen)) return next;  // CAS; false = someone else won
}
throw new TooMuchContentionException();

// Pessimistic: lock the one key, check and write inside.
ReentrantLock l = locks.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ReentrantLock());
l.lock();
try {
    ShowSeat s = repo.find(key).orElseThrow();
    s.hold(user, ttl, clock);        // throws if unavailable
    repo.save(s);
} finally { l.unlock(); }

The Backstop That Actually Holds

Both of the above live in one JVM. Deploy a second replica and the ReentrantLock prevents nothing, silently — the failure mode is that it works perfectly in every test and breaks the day you scale out.

So the answer includes: "and a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) where status = BOOKED. The in-process lock stops double-booking in one JVM; the constraint is what stops it in three." Say it even when the interview is explicitly single-process — it costs one sentence and it's the difference between a design that passes the round and one that survives deployment.

Note that the DB-level versions of both strategies are the same two ideas: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is pessimistic, a version column with UPDATE ... WHERE version = ? is optimistic, and the constraint sits underneath both.

Failure Mode

"Optimistic is the modern choice." It's better under low contention and strictly worse on a hot row.

Unbounded retry loops. An optimistic retry with no cap turns contention into a livelock and a CPU spike.

Omitting the constraint because it's "an in-memory design."

Connections

  • Previous: 27-identify-the-contended-resource.md
  • Next: 29-lock-granularity.md
  • Lighter alternative: 30-concurrenthashmap-atomics.md — when the whole decision fits on one key.
  • Worked: ../../07-Design-problems/high-concurrency-flash-sale-system.md — the scale where optimistic definitively loses.

notes.title: Lock Granularity
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The formula? A lock covering n independent resources with a critical section of t seconds caps them at 1/t ops/s combined.
Per-seat vs per-show? Per-show serialises a 300-seat house at one booking at a time.
How do you create per-key locks? locks.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ReentrantLock()) — lock striping.
The cost of fine locks? More locks to acquire in multi-resource operations → ordering discipline (→ item 31).
What must you always state? The throughput consequence of the granularity you chose.

The 30-Second Answer

Granularity is a number, not a preference. If the critical section takes t and the lock covers n independent resources, you've capped those n at 1/t operations per second in total. A 100 µs critical section under one global lock is 10,000 ops/s for the entire system; under a per-seat lock it's 10,000 ops/s per seat, and seats are independent. Quoting that ratio turns "I'd use finer locks" into a defended decision.

Cap = 1 / t per lock. One lock over n independent resources shares that cap across all n.

Choosing the Key

The lock key should be the smallest thing whose invariant you're protecting — which is usually the same key you'd put a unique constraint on.

Design Right key Wrong key, and why
BookMyShow (showId, seatId) showId — serialises a full house
Parking lot spotId levelId — serialises a floor of a busy garage
Elevator elevatorId the bank — cars are independent
Inventory skuId the warehouse
Splitwise the ordered (userA, userB) pair the group — unrelated pairs block each other 
// Lock striping: one lock per key, created on demand.
private final ConcurrentHashMap<SeatKey, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

private ReentrantLock lockFor(SeatKey k) {
    return locks.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ReentrantLock());
}

One caveat worth volunteering: this map grows with the key space and nothing removes entries. At interview scale that's fine — say so. At real scale you'd use a fixed stripe array (locks[key.hashCode() & (STRIPES-1)]), which caps memory and accepts that unrelated keys occasionally share a lock. Naming that trade — unbounded precision vs bounded memory — is a good sentence.

The Two Failure Directions

Too coarse is the common one and it's a throughput bug that no test catches, because tests are single-threaded. It shows up as a latency shelf under load.

Too fine is rarer but real: locking two things that must move together — the LRU's map and its recency list, or a seat and the booking count — means an observer can see one updated and not the other. If two structures share an invariant, they share a lock. That's a correctness argument, and it overrides the throughput one.

Failure Mode

One synchronized service method. State the consequence or narrow it.

Choosing granularity without naming throughput. The number is the argument.

Splitting a lock across an invariant. Fine-grained is not free; two locks over one invariant is a correctness bug.

Connections

  • Previous: 28-optimistic-vs-pessimistic-locking.md
  • Next: 30-concurrenthashmap-atomics.md
  • Consequence: 31-deadlock-avoidance-by-lock-ordering.md — fine locks mean multi-lock operations.

notes.title: ConcurrentHashMap.compute / putIfAbsent as the Atomic Primitive
notes.html:
Reference Links

  • The contract: non-blocking retrievals, per-key atomic updates, and the constraints on the remapping function — Java SE 21 API: ConcurrentHashMap

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What's atomic? The whole compute / computeIfAbsent / putIfAbsent invocation, per key.
What's not? if (map.get(k) == null) map.put(k, v) — two atomic ops with a race between them.
Constraint on the function? Short, non-blocking, no I/O, and it must not touch another key of the same map.
When does this replace a lock? When the entire decision fits on one key.
When doesn't it? Anything spanning two keys or two structures → explicit lock (→ items 29, 31).

The 30-Second Answer

Most interview-scale atomicity is achievable without an explicit lock. compute runs your remapping function while holding that key's bin lock, so the check and the write cannot interleave — which closes the check-then-act race directly, in one expression. The constraint is that the function must be fast and must not reach outside that key.

The Contract, Precisely

The javadoc is worth being able to paraphrase: retrievals (including get) generally do not block and reflect the results of the most recently completed update operations. Updates via compute/computeIfAbsent/merge are atomic for their key — the remapping function is evaluated under the bin's lock, so no other thread can observe or interleave a half-done update for that key.

Two consequences that are the actual exam material:

Blocking inside the function blocks other threads. Anything hashing to the same bin waits. So: no I/O, no gateway calls, no acquiring another lock.

Touching the same map inside the function is a documented way to deadlock yourself. map.compute(a, (k,v) -> map.get(b)) is not safe. If the decision needs two keys, you need a lock (item 29), not a cleverer compute.

In Practice

// The atomic hold — no explicit lock, and lazy expiry folded in for free.
public boolean tryHold(SeatKey key, UserId user) {
    Hold result = holds.compute(key, (k, existing) -> {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        boolean free = existing == null || now.isAfter(existing.expiresAt());
        return free ? new Hold(user, now.plus(ttl)) : existing;
    });
    return result.userId().equals(user);
}

// Atomic counter decrement with a floor — flash-sale stock, no lock.
public boolean tryReserve(SkuId sku, int qty) {
    Integer after = stock.computeIfPresent(sku, (k, n) -> n >= qty ? n - qty : n);
    return after != null && after % 1 == 0 && ... ;   // see note below
}

// Cleaner: merge with an explicit sentinel, or compute returning the decision via the value.
public boolean reserve(SkuId sku, int qty) {
    var outcome = new boolean[1];
    stock.compute(sku, (k, n) -> {
        if (n != null && n >= qty) { outcome[0] = true; return n - qty; }
        outcome[0] = false; return n;
    });
    return outcome[0];
}

The counter example shows the awkward part honestly: compute returns the value, not whether your branch was taken, so communicating the decision out takes either an encoding in the value (as tryHold does — return the winner's hold and compare) or a one-element array. Both are fine; pick one and say why. It's a real ergonomic cost of the lock-free approach and mentioning it reads as experience.

putIfAbsent is the simpler sibling: atomic create-if-missing, returning the previous value or null. It's the right tool for lock striping (locks.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ReentrantLock())) and for idempotency-key insertion in memory.

Failure Mode

"ConcurrentHashMap makes my code thread-safe." It makes each operation atomic. Composed operations are still races.

Slow work inside compute — a gateway call in there stalls every key in that bin.

Using it for multi-key invariants. Group booking spans N seats; that's lock ordering (item 31), not compute.

Connections

  • Previous: 29-lock-granularity.md
  • Next: 31-deadlock-avoidance-by-lock-ordering.md
  • Used by: ../01-requirements-and-scoping/05-in-memory-first-rule.md — the map is storage; this is what makes transitions safe.
  • Deeper: Java index #29 — CHM internals. Link, don't re-derive.

notes.title: Deadlock Avoidance by Lock Ordering
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The standard answer? Acquire locks in a global total order — sort by ID before locking.
Why does it work? A cycle requires someone holding a higher ID while waiting on a lower one. A consistent order makes that impossible.
The two canonical setups? Two-account transfer; group seat booking.
What else do you add? tryLock with a timeout, and release in reverse order in a finally.
Why is this asked? Because it has a clean memorable answer — it's a check, not a puzzle.

The 30-Second Answer

Group A locks seats 1 and 2 and wants 3; group B locks 3 and wants 2. Neither yields. Sort the seat IDs before acquiring and the cycle becomes impossible, because every thread walks the same direction through the ordering. State it as the general rule rather than the specific fix — the interviewer's next problem is the same shape.

In Practice

public void bookAll(List<SeatKey> seats, UserId user) throws InterruptedException {
    List<SeatKey> ordered = seats.stream().sorted().toList();     // ← the whole answer
    Deque<ReentrantLock> held = new ArrayDeque<>();
    try {
        for (SeatKey k : ordered) {
            ReentrantLock l = locks.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ReentrantLock());
            if (!l.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))            // bounded wait
                throw new SeatsUnavailableException(k);
            held.push(l);
        }
        ordered.forEach(k -> reserve(k, user));                    // all-or-nothing
    } finally {
        while (!held.isEmpty()) held.pop().unlock();               // reverse order
    }
}

Three details beyond the sort, each worth a sentence:

tryLock with a timeout. Ordering prevents deadlock among well-behaved participants; a bounded wait also protects against a thread that stalls while holding a lock, and it converts an availability failure into a clean retryable "seats unavailable."

Release in reverse, in a finally. A partial acquisition that throws must not leak locks.

SeatKey needs a total order — implement Comparable over (showId, seatId). "Sort by ID" quietly assumes an ordering exists; saying which one shows you've actually written it.

Where It Stops Working

Across processes the in-process lock isn't the mechanism at all. Two options, and a preference worth defending:

  • One DB transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over the ordered seat set. All-or-nothing for free, the ordering argument still applies to the row locks, one fewer piece of infrastructure. Preferred.
  • A distributed lock (Redis, fencing token, TTL shorter than the hold). Right when the work inside can't be a database transaction.

The thing to monitor is hold-to-confirm conversion by group size. If five-seat groups convert far worse than singles, you're losing them to lock timeouts — and that's invisible in every other metric.

Failure Mode

Locking in list order. The list order is the user's click order, which is arbitrary — that is the deadlock.

Blocking lock() with no timeout. No deadlock, but one stalled thread becomes an unbounded stall for everyone behind it.

Assuming an ordering exists. Say what the total order is.

Connections

  • Previous: 30-concurrenthashmap-atomics.md
  • Next: 32-idempotency-keys.md
  • Caused by: 29-lock-granularity.md — fine locks mean multi-lock operations.
  • Worked: ../../07-Design-problems/book-my-show.md — group booking.

notes.title: Idempotency Keys
notes.html:
Reference Links

  • The industry reference contract — stored first result, parameter fingerprinting, retention window — Stripe API: Idempotent requests

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why doesn't a lock fix a double-charge? The retry arrives after the first request finished and released everything. It's repetition, not interleaving.
The mechanism? Client-generated key; server stores the first result and replays it for the same key.
The critical ordering detail? Insert the key before the side effect, in the same transaction, guarded by a unique constraint.
Does a stored failure replay? Yes — including a 500. That's the point: the outcome is fixed at first execution.
Retention? Finite. Stripe prunes keys after ≥ 24 hours; a reused pruned key becomes a new request.
What about a gateway timeout? The honest state is PAYMENT_UNKNOWN, not FAILED. Reconcile by querying with your own reference.

The 30-Second Answer

A timed-out payment is not a race and no lock helps — the client will retry, and the retry is a legitimate, well-formed second request that must not become a second purchase. The fix is a client-supplied idempotency key: the server records it with the result of the first execution and returns that stored result for every subsequent request carrying the same key.

The Contract Worth Copying

Stripe's implementation is the reference, and four of its properties are the answer to the follow-up questions:

  1. The first result is stored whether it succeeded or failed — a retry after a 500 returns the same 500 rather than re-executing. The outcome is frozen at first execution.
  2. Incoming parameters are fingerprinted and compared against the original; a mismatch errors, so a key can't be reused for a different operation.
  3. Keys are client-generated, V4 UUID suggested, up to 255 characters, and should not carry sensitive data.
  4. Keys are prunable after at least 24 hours. The guarantee has a window; a retry arriving after it is a fresh operation.

In Practice

public PaymentResult pay(String idempotencyKey, PaymentRequest req) {
    try {
        keyStore.insert(idempotencyKey, req.fingerprint());   // UNIQUE(idempotency_key)
    } catch (DuplicateKeyException dup) {
        StoredResult prior = keyStore.get(idempotencyKey);
        if (!prior.fingerprint().equals(req.fingerprint()))
            throw new IdempotencyKeyReusedException();        // same key, different request
        return prior.result();                               // replay, including a stored failure
    }
    PaymentResult r = gateway.charge(req);                   // may time out → PAYMENT_UNKNOWN
    keyStore.recordResult(idempotencyKey, r);
    return r;
}

The insert precedes the charge, and the unique constraint — not the check — is what makes it safe. A if (keyStore.exists(k)) check before the insert is the same check-then-act race as everywhere else; the constraint is what closes it, and a concurrent duplicate loses there rather than at a read.

The TTL relationship matters too. The hold must outlive the payment timeout with margin:

holdTtl > gateway p99 + gateway timeout + retry budget + clock skew

If the seat hold expires at 5 minutes and the gateway can hang for 6, you've built a system that charges people for seats it already resold. Five to ten minutes is conventional; saying the inequality rather than the number shows you know what would break it.

Reconciliation. On a timeout the state is PAYMENT_UNKNOWN. It resolves by querying the gateway with your own reference on a retry schedule, and the booking sits there until it does. Marking it FAILED and releasing the seat is the mistake that produces the worst customer outcome available.

Failure Mode

Reaching for a lock. Locks solve interleaving; keys solve repetition. Confusing them is common and very visible.

Inserting the key after the side effect. The crash window between charge and record is exactly the case the key exists for.

Treating a timeout as a failure. It's an unknown.

Connections

  • Previous: 31-deadlock-avoidance-by-lock-ordering.md
  • Next: 33-reservation-with-ttl-hold-then-confirm.md
  • Appears in: ../01-requirements-and-scoping/04-api-first-sketch.md — confirm(token, idempotencyKey).

notes.title: Reservation with TTL / Hold-Then-Confirm

headings.text: The Two Expiry Paths, and Why Both

notes.html:
Reference Links

  • Injected time, without which none of this is testable — Java SE 21 API: java.time.Clock

Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three states? AVAILABLE → HELD (with expiry) → BOOKED. Plus expiry back to AVAILABLE.
Lazy expiry or sweeper? Both, for different reasons. Lazy makes it correct; the sweeper makes availability visible.
Why is lazy the correctness one? Next reader compares now to expiresAt — a stale hold can never block a booking, even if the sweeper is down.
The TTL lower bound? > gateway p99 + timeout + retry budget + clock skew. Conventionally 5–10 min.
What breaks if TTL < payment timeout? You charge for seats you already released.
Which problems share this? BookMyShow (#49), e-commerce cart (#50), hotel/airline (#53), flash sale, any slot booking.

The 30-Second Answer

Inventory that's paid for asynchronously can't go straight from available to sold — there's a window where it's neither. Model that window explicitly as a HELD state carrying a holder and an expiry, and make expiry evaluated lazily on read so correctness doesn't depend on a background job running. Add a sweeper on top so the seat map displays correctly, and be clear those are two different requirements.

The sweeper only fixes what the seat map shows; correctness comes from checking expiresAt on every read.

The Two Expiry Paths, and Why Both

Lazy expiry-on-read is the correctness mechanism. Any reader compares now against expiresAt and treats an expired hold as absent — so a stale hold can never block a booking, even if every background thread is dead. It costs nothing and it folds directly into the atomic claim:

holds.compute(key, (k, existing) -> {
    Instant now = clock.instant();
    boolean free = existing == null || now.isAfter(existing.expiresAt());   // lazy expiry
    return free ? new Hold(user, now.plus(ttl)) : existing;
});

The sweeper is a UX mechanism. Without it the seat map shows an expired seat as taken until somebody happens to try it, which looks broken. It's a ScheduledExecutorService pass that clears expired entries and pushes an availability update (→ item 34).

Candidates usually name one. Naming both and separating their purposes — correctness vs visibility — is the stronger answer, and it also answers "what if the sweeper thread dies?" before it's asked: nothing breaks, the display goes stale.

The Rest of the Lifecycle

AVAILABLE ──hold(user,ttl)──► HELD ──confirm(user)──► BOOKED
    ▲                          │                        │
    └──release() / expiry──────┘                        └──(cancellation, if in scope)

Three invariants the entity enforces (→ item 10): you cannot be BOOKED without having been HELD; you cannot confirm someone else's hold; you cannot confirm an expired one. All three are confirm()'s preconditions, and all three are one-line tests once Clock is injected.

TTL sizing is the number the interviewer will push on. The inequality is the answer: it must exceed the payment gateway's p99 plus its timeout plus your retry budget plus clock skew. Conventional values are 5–10 minutes because payment flows are conventionally under a minute; quoting the inequality rather than "ten minutes" is what shows you know what would break it.

Group holds are all-or-nothing over N seats, which drags in lock ordering (→ item 31), and the TTL applies to the group, not per seat.

Failure Mode

No distinction between "held" and "booked." The flagship BookMyShow modelling failure — the seat is either free or sold, and the payment window has nowhere to live.

Sweeper-only expiry. There's a window where a genuinely expired seat reads as taken, and the whole design's correctness now depends on a background thread.

Instant.now() inside the expiry check. The behaviour is right and untestable (→ item 38).

TTL shorter than the payment timeout. The worst available outcome: charged, no seat.

notes.title: Background Schedulers
notes.html:
Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The tool? ScheduledExecutorService — scheduleAtFixedRate or scheduleWithFixedDelay.
Difference between the two? Fixed rate measures period start-to-start and can bunch up if a run overruns; fixed delay waits the gap after each run finishes.
Which for a sweeper? scheduleWithFixedDelay — no bunching if a pass is slow.
What happens on an uncaught exception? The task is cancelled silently and never runs again. Wrap the body in try/catch.
Shutdown? shutdown() then awaitTermination(), with shutdownNow() as the fallback.
What must the sweeper not be? The correctness mechanism (→ item 33).

The 30-Second Answer

Expiry sweeps, elevator step ticks and retry passes all run on a ScheduledExecutorService. Three things get asked about: which scheduling method and why, what happens when a run throws, and how it shuts down. The silent-cancellation behaviour on an uncaught exception is the one most people don't know, and it's the reason a sweeper "just stops working" in production.

Wrap the body in try/catch and log: that one habit is the difference between a sweeper and a sweeper that quietly stopped.

In Practice

public final class HoldSweeper implements AutoCloseable {
    private final ScheduledExecutorService exec =
            Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> {
                Thread t = new Thread(r, "hold-sweeper");
                t.setDaemon(true);                        // doesn't block JVM exit
                return t;
            });

    public void start() {
        // fixed DELAY: if a sweep is slow, the next one doesn't pile on top of it
        exec.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::sweepSafely, 30, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    }

    private void sweepSafely() {
        try {
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            holds.entrySet().removeIf(e -> now.isAfter(e.getValue().expiresAt()));
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            log.error("sweep failed", e);   // MUST catch: an escaped exception
        }                                   // cancels all future runs, silently
    }

    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        exec.shutdown();
        if (!exec.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) exec.shutdownNow();
    }
}

The three follow-ups and their answers.

Rate vs delay: fixed rate targets start times, so a run that overruns its period causes the next to fire immediately and successive runs to bunch. Fixed delay measures from completion, which is what you want for a sweep whose duration varies with backlog. Say which and why.

Missed ticks: an elevator that steps every 500 ms and misses a tick because of GC or a slow step must not "catch up" by taking two steps instantly — it should advance by elapsed time, or skip. This is the same argument as fixed-rate bunching, applied to simulation.

Shutdown: shutdown() stops accepting new tasks and lets running ones finish; awaitTermination bounds the wait; shutdownNow interrupts. A daemon thread means the JVM can still exit if you forget, which is a safety net, not a design.

The elevator case is the other use: the control loop is a scheduled tick that advances each car by one step. Worth noting that this makes the elevator autonomous — it moves without a request arriving — which is what makes it the hardest of the classic LLD problems.

Failure Mode

Unguarded task body. An uncaught exception cancels the schedule permanently and silently. This is the single most valuable fact in this note.

scheduleAtFixedRate for a variable-duration job. Runs bunch under load, exactly when you least want them to.

Making the sweeper load-bearing. Correctness must come from lazy expiry (→ item 33); the sweeper is for visibility.

No shutdown story. "How does this stop?" is a standard follow-up.
